questions.question: How do you implement a stack and a queue with Go slices?
questions.title: How do you implement a stack and a queue with Go slices
questions.direct_answer: A stack removes the most recently added item, while a queue removes the earliest. A Go slice supports stack push and pop at the end; a simple queue appends at the end and advances from the front. Push uses `append`. Stack pop reads `s[len(s)-1]` and shortens to `s[:len(s)-1]`. Queue dequeue reads `s[0]` and shortens to `s[1:]`, after checking for emptiness.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A stack removes the most recently added item, while a queue removes the earliest. A Go slice supports stack push and pop at the end; a simple queue appends at the end and advances from the front.

Push uses `append`. Stack pop reads `s[len(s)-1]` and shortens to `s[:len(s)-1]`. Queue dequeue reads `s[0]` and shortens to `s[1:]`, after checking for emptiness.

For example, pushing `10`, then `20` gives stack `[10 20]`; popping returns `20`. Enqueuing the same values and dequeuing returns `10` because a queue is first-in, first-out.

Every pop or dequeue must define empty behaviour. These basic containers are not safe for concurrent access without synchronization, and copying a slice value still shares its backing storage.

A slice is the simplest choice for an in-memory stack and for a small or short-lived queue. It is idiomatic, cache-friendly, and needs no node allocation.

sections.title: The core model: using slices as stacks and queues
sections.content:
using slices as stacks and queues is easiest to understand by following the data or control from input to result. The details below form one connected model rather than a list of unrelated rules.

The slice header tracks a pointer, length, and capacity. Stack operations at the end align naturally with this representation and are amortized O(1). A front reslice is also O(1) because it changes the header, but that does not mean the unused prefix has been released to the allocator.

sections.title: using slices as stacks and queues example
using slices as stacks and queues at a glance
sections.content:
| Operation | Slice expression | Typical cost |
|---|---|---:|
| Stack push | `s = append(s, x)` | Amortized O(1) |
| Stack pop | `x; s = s[:len(s)-1]` | O(1) |
| Queue enqueue | `q = append(q, x)` | Amortized O(1) |
| Simple dequeue | `x; q = q[1:]` | O(1), may retain array |

sections.title: The practical decision: using slices as stacks and queues
sections.content:
The useful question is not whether using slices as stacks and queues can be used, but which requirement makes it the clearest and safest fit. That decision includes its cost and its failure boundary.

For parsing, DFS, undo history, and other local stacks, a slice is normally ideal. A short request-local queue is also fine. A service queue that lives for hours, holds large objects, or has a fixed capacity deserves a head index, compaction rule, or circular buffer so memory behaviour stays predictable.

sections.title: Why the failure happens: using slices as stacks and queues
sections.content:
Failures around using slices as stacks and queues usually come from one incorrect assumption about ownership, state, ordering, or lifetime. Finding that assumption is more useful than adding a defensive line at random.

A tiny remaining subslice can keep an entire large backing array reachable. Clearing the removed slot breaks references to its value, but the array itself remains until no slice points to it. Compaction copies live elements into a fresh or reset region when the consumed prefix becomes large.

sections.title: The important trade-off: using slices as stacks and queues
sections.content:
using slices as stacks and queues and a linked or circular queue solve related problems, but they expose different guarantees. The best choice follows from the guarantee the program actually needs.

A circular buffer stores head, tail, and size and wraps indexes at capacity. It provides bounded storage and stable O(1) enqueue/dequeue, but full-versus-empty state needs careful handling. A growing slice is less code and adapts its capacity, which is often the right trade for interview basics.

sections.title: A reliable diagnosis: using slices as stacks and queues
sections.content:
A good investigation traces the first point where the real state differs from the expected state. With using slices as stacks and queues, that means observing the relevant input, transition, and result rather than guessing from the final symptom.

A small container API can return `(T, bool)` for empty operations and zero the removed slot for reference-containing types. Tests should cover empty, one item, wrap or compaction boundaries, alternating operations, and preservation of FIFO or LIFO order. A mutex belongs around the whole invariant if multiple goroutines share it.
